on 2 July, 2024

 In The High Court Of Punjab And Haryana

M/S K.B. Foods
 ......Petitioner
 Versus
Punjab State Power Corporation Limited And Others
 .......Respondents 
Coram : Hon'Ble Mr. Justice Vinod S. Bhardwaj

Present: - Mr. Vijay Lath, Advocate
 for the petitioner. 
 ** ** *
Vinod S. Bhardwaj, J. (Oral) 
1.  The instant writ petition has been filed for seeking directions to be used to the respondents to release a new commercial electricity connection with load of 48 KV in the premises of the petitioner with trade mark of "TANDOORI BITES" situated at Village Khajurala, Tehsil Phagwara, District Kapurthala. 
2. Counsel for the petitioner contends that the petitioner is a partnership firm having its registered office at 2-A/124, Shankar Garden, Near Income Tax Colony, District Jalandhar and is running a Restaurant under the trade mark of "Tandoori Bites" situated at Village 1 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 Khajurala, Tehsil Phagwara, District Kapurthala. He contends that the establishment started after executing a lease agreement dated 04.03.2003 with the then owner of the land. The Construction was thereafter, raised by the petitioner after spending huge amount and as per the terms and conditions of the lease agreement and for the purpose specified thereunder. 
With a gradual growth of business, more area of land was required and an additional fresh lease M/S K.B. Foods vs Punjab State Power Corporation Limited ... on 2 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65847261/
1 agreement was executed on 11.08.2005. It is submitted that the petitioner continued to occupy the said premises and there has been no default in payment of any statutory dues and/or contractual obligations on the part of the petitioner. The original lessor namely, Naib Singh received entire lease money during his life time, however, he died in the year 2011 whereupon his estate was inherited by his widow, daughter and son and that they have been receiving the lease money in terms of the settlement as agreed between the parties. 
3. Eventually, the LRs of Naib Singh sold the land to one Apinder Singh Nijjar vide sale deed dated 03.03.2020 whereupon, he became the lessor of the lease premises. The said lessor is a resident of U.S.A and one Kuljit Singh Bahia claims himself to be the attorney of said Apinder Singh Nijjar and it is contended that he started interfering in the lease premises of the petitioner, without any authority and legal justification and with a malicious intent to oust the petitioner. 
4. Aggrieved thereof, a suit was filed for declaration claiming that the petitioner is a lessee of the suit premises alongwith a prayer of an injunction to direct the respondents being successor-in-interest of suit 2 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 property to get registered or execute registered lease deed/rent deed in favour of the petitioner with a further relief of a permanent injunction to restrain them from interfering the premises has also been sought. The said Civil Suit No. 20 of 2022 dated 18.10.2022 is pending before the Civil Judge (Junior Division), Phagwara. The hearing in the said case is fixed to 17.07.2024. He contends that Kuljit Singh Bahia claiming himself to be the attorney of Apinder Singh Nijjar started interfering in the premises of which the petitioner is in an undisputed occupation with a mala fide intention and to forcibly grab the property by dispossessing the petitioner in an unlawful manner in connivance with the officials of the Punjab Police. 
5. Additionally, a Criminal Writ Petition No. 10255 of 2021 was also filed by the petitioner before this Court seeking protection of his life and liberty. The Inspector General of Police, Jalandhar Range was directed by this Court vide Order dated 28.10.2021 to look into the matter and to file his personal affidavit whereupon the affidavit was submitted. The said Criminal Writ Petition is stated to be still pending. He contends that the lessor, through his attorney, thereafter got the sanctioned load reduced from 90 KV to 1 KV which has caused severe prejudice to the petitioner in carrying out his day to day operations. 
6. Considering that a higher load was required by it for operating the heavy electric/electronic equipments such as Deep Freezers, Refrigerators, Heavy Voltage Air Conditioners, Bear Making Machines as well as the necessary ventilation and lighting equipments, an application was thereafter, submitted by the petitioner for seeking release of a new 3 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 commercial electricity connection with a load of 48 KV on 16.05.2024 and an application in this regard has been duly furnished. It is also submitted that the electricity Department had already appeared in the said Civil Suit and filed a written statement stating therein that the petitioner not being a Consumer as per their record, hence, he cannot seek change of the load on the pending electricity meter. Hence, the application seeking restoration of the earlier commercial electricity load was dismissed by Civil Judge (Junior Division), Jalandhar. The said order passed by the Civil Judge (Junior Division), Jalandhar has not been challenged by the M/S K.B. Foods vs Punjab State Power Corporation Limited ... on 2 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65847261/
2 petitioner before any Court. Further, no separate application has been filed by the petitioner for seeking release of a fresh connection in the pending application. Instead, the petitioner submitted an application for new commercial electricity connection with the respondents but the same was allegedly not accepted by the official respondents by orally averring that a Court case is pending and as such they will not accept the application of the petitioner for release of a new commercial electricity connection. The said application was accordingly sent through a registered post on 03.06.2024 for issuance of a new commercial electricity connection. 
7. The Counsel on behalf of petitioner has approached this Court by averring that in view of the judgment of this Court in the matter "Mobin Ansari versus Punjab State Power Corporation Limited and others"
(2022(4) R.C.R (Civil) 782) as well as the subsequent judgment in the matter of "Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited versus Punjab State Power Corporation Limited and others"(2023(3) R.C.R (Civil)306, the 4 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 petitioner is entitled to release of electricity connection since he is in an authorized and is in permissive possession of the premises in question under a valid lease agreement executed with him and that he cannot be dispossessed except a due process of law. The denial of the basic amenities to the petitioner cannot be permitted as a mode of seeking eviction of the petitioner from the premises in question as the same is likely to promote illegitimate means for seeking eviction of an occupant of the premises. 
8. A specific question posed to the petitioner as regards the pendency of the Civil Suit and as to why the provisions of Order 2 Rule 2 of CPC would not be applicable especially when the suit was for permanent injunction to restrain the defendants/officials from disconnecting/changing the active load of the electricity connection bearing Account No. 3007557693 alongwith mandatory injunction for directing the restoration of the total electricity load was already pending and was subjudice. 
9. Responding to the above, the Counsel for the petitioner submits that the suit was only for mandatory injunction and that the reduction in load was subsequent to the institution of the suit. 
10. The said reply is erroneous on the facts of the case and is apparently an attempt to mislead this Court. The head note of the amended plaint appended by the petitioner alongwith instant writ petition as Annexure P-32 clearly shows that the suit was filed by the petitioner for permanent injunction to restrain the defendants, which includes the officials of the Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. as well as the subsequent lessor from disconnecting/changing the active load of the electricity connection bearing 5 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 Account No.
3007557693 and old meter connection No. 300607045. Thus, the cause of action for seeking relief against any change in the active load of the said electricity connection had already been invoked in the above said Civil Suit. Additionally, an application was also filed for seeking restoration of the said electricity connection and load which was dismissed by the Civil Court. The petitioner has a remedy available to him either to impugn the said order passed by the Civil Judge (Junior Division),
Jalandhar before the Appellate Court or to move an appropriate application for an appropriate M/S K.B. Foods vs Punjab State Power Corporation Limited ... on 2 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65847261/
3 interim relief of seeking release of a new electricity connection in view of the position in law relied upon by the petitioner and as laid down by this Court. The needful was however, not done and he instead is portraying the same as a new cause of action, despite an unsuccessful attempt of seeking restoration of the supply. Besides, the head note of the plaint clearly contemplates the change in the electricity connection as well as load and a restrain order was sought by the petitioner apart from a separate application seeking restoration. The claim having been already raised, failure on the part of the petitioner in securing the desired relief from Civil Court would not give a fresh cause of action to elect a different forum for the redressal of the same grievance for which he has failed to secure a favourable order in the suit before the Competent Court. 
11. Even otherwise if the contention of the petitioner is considered for the sake of arguments that the bar of Order 2 Rule 2 of CPC would not be applicable, yet, the issue in question would at best relate to release a fresh electricity connection and that as per the provisions of forum and 6 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 ombudsman regulation, the alternative remedy under Section 42 (5) of the Electricity Act read with Section 42 (7) of the Electricity Act have already been prescribed before a statutory body by the name and style of Consumer Grievances redressal forum and the electricity Ombudsman thereafter. 
Reliance in this regard may be placed in the matter of "Harmit Singh and another versus State of Punjab and others" passed in CWP-9901-2023 dated 08.05.2023. The relevant extract is reproduced as under:
4. Section 42 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides for establishment of a Forum for redressal of grievances of consumers and the authority to be known as Ombudsman. 
The relevant provisions of Section 42 of the Electricity Act are reproduced hereinafter below:-
"Section 42. (Duties of distribution licensee and open access): -
(1) It shall be the duty of a distribution licensee to develop and maintain an efficient,
co-ordinated and economical distribution system in his area of supply and to supply electricity in accordance with the provisions contained in this Act.
xxx xxx xxx ( 5 ) Every distribution licensee shall, within six months from the appointed date or date of grant of licence, whichever is earlier, establish a forum for redressal of grievances of the consumers in accordance with the guidelines as may be specified by the State Commission. 
(6) Any consumer, who is aggrieved by non- redressal of his grievances under sub-section (5), may make a representation for the redressal of his 7 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 grievance to an authority to be known as Ombudsman to be appointed or designated by the State Commission.

4 (7) The Ombudsman shall settle the grievance of the consumer within such time and in such manner as may be specified by the State Commission." 
5. The Punjab Electricity Regulatory Commission in exercise of the powers conferred upon it by Section 181 read with Sections 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 50, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 126, 127, 135, 152, 154 and 163 of the Electricity Act, 2003 notified the Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission (Electricity Supply Code and Related matters), Regulations 2014. Clause 25 of the aforesaid Electricity Supply Code deals with the complaint's redressal system. The relevant provision reads thus:-
"25.3 Forum for Redressal of Grievances of the Consumers Any complainant aggrieved by non-redressal of his grievance by the distribution licensee and/or under the Consumer Complaint Handling Procedure, as the case may be, may himself or through his authorized representative, approach the Forum established by the distribution licensee as per PSERC (Forum and Ombudsman) Regulations, 2005 as amended from time to time, in writing for the redressal of his grievance. Provided that the complainant shall have the right to approach the Forum directly in respect of matters falling under the jurisdiction of the Forum. 
25.4 Redressal of Grievances by Ombudsman 25.4.1 A complainant aggrieved by an order of the 8 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 Forum or non-redressal of grievance by the Forum within the prescribed period shall have the right to submit an appeal to the Ombudsman. 
25.4.2 A consumer may submit a representation to the Ombudsman if any order passed by a Dispute Settlement Committee, Forum or Ombudsman is not implemented within 30 days of the receipt of such order. 
6. The Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission has also approved the guidelines for handling of consumer complaints and speedy resolution of consumer grievances relating to supply of electricity by the distribution licensee to the consumers in a transparent and expeditious manner and vide notification dated 04.10.2013 approved "Consumer Complaint Handling Procedure (CCHP)" as well. The relevant provisions are reproduced as under:-

xxx xxx xxx " 8 . Consumer's right to approach the Forum A complainant aggrieved due to non-redressal of his complaint under the "Consumer Complaint Handling Procedure", may approach the Forum established by the licensee under sub-section (5) of Section 42 of the Act read with "PSERC (Forum & Ombudsman) Regulations,
2005" as amended from time to time." 
7. Detailed procedure for institution of complaint and redressal of the complaint had also been provided under the above said guidelines. 
8. Thereafter, the Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission vide notification dated 26.12.2016,in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 181 and other provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003 notified The Punjab State Electricity and Regulatory Commission (Forum &
Ombudsman) Regulations of 2016 which provide for detailed mechanism for adjudication of disputes. The grievance for release of New Connection is within the scope of such authorities. The relevant provisions of the said Regulations are reproduced:
(d) "Complainant" means & includes any of the 10 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 following who have a grievance as defined in these regulations and makes a complaint;

(f) "consumer" for the purpose of these Regulations shall be a consumer as defined under sub-section (15) of Section 2 of the Act and shall also include a person applying for new connection;
(g) "consumer grievance" means & includes any complaint relating to any fault, imperfection, short coming, defect or deficiency in the quality, nature and manner of service or performance in pursuance of a licence, contract, agreement or under Electricity Supply Code or in relation to Standards of Performance specified by the Commission including payment of compensation or billing disputes of any nature or recovery of charges by the licensee and matters relating to the safety of the distribution system having potential of endangering the life or property. However, the matters pertaining to Open Access granted under the Act and Section 126, 127, 135 to 140, 142, 143, 146, 152 and 161 of the Act shall not form grievance under these regulations.

significance of such essential requirement should not be minimized by the practitioners of law.
High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India is plenary in nature, not limited to any other provision of the Constitution.
Prior exhaustion of alternate remedy is a rule of prudence and not of compulsion.
In the absence of the circumstances noticed above, a writ jurisdiction would not be panacea for all the maladies which a litigant may suffer.
Therefore, when a statutory forum is created by law for redressal of grievances, a writ petition should not be entertained ignoring the statutory dispensation.
The burden lies on the person approaching the Writ Court to explain as to 31 of 33 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:082377 why,despite existence of a specialized statutory remedy,
the High Court still ought to exercise its writ jurisdiction.
One of the restrictions placed on the power of the High Court is where an effective alternate remedy is available to the aggrieved person;
(ii) Exceptions to the rule of alternate remedy arise where (a) the writ petition has been filed for the enforcement of a fundamental right protected by Part III of the Constitution; (b) there has been a violation of the principles of natural justice; (c) the order or proceedings are wholly without jurisdiction; or (d) the vires of a legislation is challenged;
(iii) An alternate remedy by itself does not divest the High Court of its powers under Article 226 of the Constitution in an appropriate case though ordinarily, a writ petition should not be entertained when an efficacious alternate remedy is provided by law;
(iv) When a right is created by a statute, which itself prescribes the remedy or procedure for enforcing the right or liability, resort must be had to that particular statutory remedy before invoking the discretionary remedy under Article 226 of the Constitution.
Considering it from either of the perspectives, the present writ petition would not be maintainable before this Court, being an attempt at forum shopping and fishing out for an interim relief, by institution of different petitions, by drawing an artificial distinction with respect to a cause of action.
